title: Understanding Reading Gaps
author: Amy Coombe
summary: Amy Coombe, writing for secondary school reading leads, offers one organising insight about struggling readers: the causes of reading difficulty are complex and varied, but reading gaps are primarily gaps in phonics, knowledge and practice, and those gaps compound over time. She uses the example of two children, Sam and Alex, who receive identical teaching yet diverge sharply because Alex needs far more repetition to learn the sound-spelling code. Because children who struggle with the code meet less text, they get less word-reading practice, which delays automatic word recognition, burdens working memory and drives avoidance of reading. She cites the Nagy and Anderson estimate that the least and most motivated middle schoolers might read 100,000 versus 10,000,000 words a year to show how large the practice gap becomes. For secondary leaders, she argues the original cause matters less than identifying present gaps and intervening with precision, urgency and intensity. She also warns that a decoding intervention alone cannot repair years of reduced reading, vocabulary and knowledge, so schools need daily reading in every subject, a knowledge-rich curriculum and explicit vocabulary teaching.
points: Reading gaps are best understood as gaps in phonics, knowledge and practice that compound, which gives secondary leaders a workable target even when the original cause of a student's difficulty is unknowable.

Children who struggle with the sound-spelling code read shorter, simpler texts, so identical time on task exposes them to far fewer words and delays the fast, automatic word recognition that frees working memory for comprehension.

The Nagy and Anderson estimate of 100,000 versus 10,000,000 words read per year by the least and most motivated readers shows how small early differences become enormous gaps in vocabulary and knowledge.
A decoding intervention is necessary but insufficient, because it cannot on its own close accumulated gaps in vocabulary, general knowledge, syntax and fluency.
Schools should pair precise intervention with reading in every subject, a knowledge-rich curriculum and systematic explicit vocabulary teaching.
quotes: The causes of reading difficulty are complex and varied, but reading gaps are primarily gaps in phonics, knowledge and practice, and the gaps compound over time.

Within the first year of school, large differences in reading practice can emerge: children who experience greater difficulty when breaking the sound-spelling code will be exposed to less text than their peers because they are still mastering the knowledge needed to read longer books.

Less word-reading practice delays the development of fast, automatic word recognition, which places greater demands on working memory and reduces capacity to understand, and make meaning from, what’s being read.

A Nagy and Anderson 1984 study, cited here, estimates that the least motivated readers in middle school might read 100,000 words a year, while the most motivated might read 10,000,000. This is a staggering gap!
Though we may not be able to identify why a student’s reading difficulties began, we can identify the gaps and do something about them.

a decoding intervention can address an important foundational gap but it cannot, on its own, make up for years of reduced reading experience or close the resulting gaps in vocabulary, general knowledge, syntactic knowledge and reading fluency.
Students need to read and read and read: every day, in every subject, at every opportunity.
